quote: Ist es etwa die Quadratwurzel aus einem Idealquadrat?
english: Is it perhaps the square root of an ideal square?
topic: The page ends a number-theoretic argument, asks how the quadratic extension obtained from the roots of a cubic equation relates to the cubic base field, and sets out a plan to apply the ideal concept to all mathematical disciplines, as Lie did with the group concept.

triage.modern_statement: This is my reading, because the note is fragmentary. Let K be a non-Galois cubic number field with discriminant d_K, and let L = K(√d_K) be the quadratic extension of K obtained by adjoining the square root of the discriminant of the cubic. L is the Galois closure, with group S3. The question seems to be whether the radicand, meaning the discriminant or the ideal it generates, is a perfect square of an ideal up to a fundamental-discriminant factor. Equivalently, it asks how L/K, and the quadratic resolvent k = Q(√d_K), relate arithmetically to the cubic field. The modern answer is the decomposition d_K = D·f², where D is the fundamental discriminant of the quadratic resolvent k and f is a conductor. In that setting L/k is a cyclic cubic extension with conductor f, and it is unramified over k exactly when f = 1.
triage.answered_by: The arithmetic of the cubic field, its quadratic resolvent and its Galois closure was fully worked out through class field theory, above all by Helmut Hasse in 'Arithmetische Theorie der kubischen Zahlkörper auf klassenkörpertheoretischer Grundlage', Math. Zeitschrift 31 (1930), 565–582. A. Scholz (1933) and later authors followed up. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Hasse, 'Arithmetische Theorie der kubischen Zahlkörper auf klassenkörpertheoretischer Grundlage', Math. Z. 31 (1930), pp. 565–582. This is the standard class-field-theoretic treatment of cubic fields.
Scholz, 'Idealklassen und Einheiten in kubischen Körpern' (1933), builds on Hasse's cubic-field theory.
Standard modern fact: Disc(K) = D(K)·F(K)², where D(K) is the discriminant of the quadratic resolvent. For an S3-cubic field this is the unique quadratic subfield of the Galois closure.
A cubic field K of discriminant D·n² has a Galois closure with group S3 that contains a unique quadratic subfield k, called the quadratic resolvent.
The cubic discriminant is decomposed as a fundamental discriminant times the square of a conductor, and this links to unramified cubic extensions of quadratic fields.

triage.why: The page context fits the question of how the quadratic extension from the roots of a cubic relates to the cubic field. The note asks whether a square root comes from an 'ideal square', which points to the fact that the cubic discriminant is a fundamental discriminant times a square (D·f²). That structure, along with the conductor and ramification of the Galois closure over the quadratic resolvent, was settled by class field theory: Hasse 1930 and follow-up work. I matched the note to this theory myself; no source discusses the note itself, and the exact object Hilbert meant by 'it' cannot be recovered with certainty. The broad area is still active: counting cubic fields with a given quadratic resolvent and the asymptotics of cubic fields are current research topics.
